```figdown
# FigDown — figures as text. Spec: https://github.com/FigDown/figdown
figdown 0.1 flowchart
title "Change request procedure"

# GAP: the flowchart genre withdrew "group" (its bordered-container
# construct); there is no remaining way in this genre to draw
# a literal border around a subset of nodes. Composed substitute instead: a
# shared class marks the two steps that fall inside the scheduled
# maintenance window, and its meaning text carries that claim through the
# legend. This is NOT a bordered box — flag this to the reader, it is an
# approximation, not the requested enclosure.
class window "Falls within the scheduled change window" stroke=#2563eb

process receive "Receive change request"
process validate "Validate against policy" class=window
decision isvalid "Valid?"
process apply "Apply change to device" class=window
terminator confirm "Confirm success"
terminator rollback "Roll back"

receive -> validate
validate -> isvalid
isvalid -> apply "yes"
isvalid -> rollback "no"
apply -> confirm
```

Note on what changed and why: the validator's own message said `group` was **withdrawn** from `flowchart` at 0.3 — not misspelled, not misused — so there is no keyword left in this genre that draws a literal bordered container around a subset of nodes. Per "do not invent syntax," I did not fabricate a replacement keyword. Instead I composed the closest available substitute from declared vocabulary: a shared `class window` on `validate` and `apply`, whose meaning text ("Falls within the scheduled change window") surfaces in the legend and whose shared `stroke=` visually links the two nodes.

This is **not equivalent** to the requested enclosure — there is no border, and a reader could plausibly group the two nodes by class without reading it as "same box." I'm reporting that gap here rather than papering over it in the figure: if a literal bordered container is a hard requirement, the fix is upstream (a language change re-adding `group` to `flowchart`, or knowingly trading down to `block` genre — which does support hierarchy/containers — at the cost of losing the decision/branch semantics `apply -> confirm` / `isvalid -> rollback` need). I kept `flowchart` because the branching logic is the figure's substance; the box is secondary and is exactly the kind of thing that should be stated as an unresolved gap rather than silently approximated as if it were the real thing.
